section_title: What happens when a warning is met with pride?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 8 The Lord has sent a message against Jacob, and it has fallen upon Israel. 9 All the people will know it— Ephraim and the dwellers of Samaria. With pride and arrogance of heart they will say: 10 “The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with finished stone; the sycamores have been felled, but we will replace them with cedars.”

11 The LORD has raised up the foes of Rezin against him and joined his enemies together. 12 Aram from the east and Philistia from the west have devoured Israel with open mouths. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.

context_lines: The focus turns to a message against Jacob and Israel, with Ephraim and Samaria named directly. These are the people of the northern kingdom. Their response to loss is proud confidence that they can replace what has fallen with something better.

The fallen bricks and felled sycamores become a boast about finished stone and cedars. The problem is the attitude expressed in the rebuilding: the people answer a warning with confidence in their own ability to recover, while refusing to face what has gone wrong before God.

The Lord raises up enemies, and Israel is attacked by Aram from the east and Philistia from the west. The closing line says His anger has not turned away and His hand remains upraised. This refrain returns in verses 17 and 21, holding the warnings together.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/9.htm) and [Wesley](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/isaiah/9.htm) understand the rebuilding speech as a refusal to be humbled. Wesley describes the speakers as expecting to repair their losses to their own advantage; Henry stresses the danger of remaining proud under circumstances meant to turn people back to God.

The [NABRE notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/isaiah/9) likewise read these verses as part of a series of judgments against the northern kingdom, with continued rebellion explaining the repeated refrain. The central issue across these readings is the people’s response to God, rather than the choice of building materials.
